questions.q_en: Which of the following is a type of mechanical wave?
questions.solution_en:
· Mechanical waves require a material medium (solid, liquid, or gas) to propagate.

· Sound waves are mechanical waves that travel via particle vibrations (e.g., air molecules compressing and rarefying).

· Why not others?

· Electromagnetic waves (e.g., light, X-rays) do not need a medium.

· Light waves are electromagnetic.

· X-rays are also electromagnetic.

questions.q_en:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?

I. In transverse waves, particle motion is perpendicular to wave propagation.

II. Sound waves can be both transverse and longitudinal.
questions.solution_en:
· Statement I (Correct):

o Transverse waves: Particle motion is perpendicular to wave direction (e.g., waves on a string, light waves).

· Statement II (Incorrect):

o Sound waves are longitudinal in gases/liquids (particles oscillate parallel to wave direction).

o Exception: In solids, sound can have both transverse and longitudinal components due to rigidity.

Example:

· Longitudinal: Sound in air (compressions/rarefactions).

· Transverse: Seismic S-waves in Earth's crust.

questions.q_en: Which property of waves is defined as the number of oscillations per second?
questions.solution_en:
· Frequency (f):

o Measured in Hertz (Hz).

o Defines oscillations per second (e.g., 50 Hz = 50 cycles/second).

· Other options:

o Wavelength: Distance between wave crests (meters).

o Amplitude: Wave height (energy measure).

o Period: Time for one oscillation (seconds).

Formula:

f=1/T ​ (where T = period).

questions.q_en: What is the SI unit of wave velocity?
questions.solution_en:
· Wave velocity (v):

o SI unit: meters per second (m/s).

o Calculated as v=f X λ (frequency X wavelength).

Example:

Speed of sound in air ≈ 343 m/s at 20°C.

questions.q_en: Sound waves in air are:
questions.solution_en:
· Longitudinal waves:

o Particles vibrate parallel to wave direction.

o In air, sound propagates as compressions (high pressure) and rarefactions (low pressure).

· Why not transverse?

o Gases/liquids lack shear rigidity for transverse waves.

o Solids can support both types.

questions.solution_en:

o The particles of the string move perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation.

o Example: Plucking a guitar string creates up-and-down oscillations.

questions.q_en: The speed of sound is highest in:
questions.solution_en:
Speed of sound depends on the medium's density and elasticity:

o Solids: Fastest speed (e.g., steel ≈ 5,960 m/s) due to tightly packed molecules and strong intermolecular forces.

o Liquids: Slower than solids (e.g., water ≈ 1,480 m/s).

o Gases: Slowest (e.g., air ≈ 343 m/s) due to widely spaced molecules.

o Vacuum: No sound (sound requires a medium to propagate).

questions.q_en: Which parameter increases when a sound source moves toward an observer?
questions.solution_en:
· Doppler Effect: When a sound source moves toward an observer:

o Frequency increases (higher pitch).

o Wavelength decreases (compressed waves).

o Speed of sound remains constant (depends only on the medium).

questions.q_en: Which of the following waves is NOT an example of an electromagnetic wave?
questions.solution_en:
Radio waves, X-rays, and Microwaves are all types of electromagnetic (EM) waves, which do not require a medium to propagate and can travel through a vacuum.

Water waves, on the other hand, are mechanical waves that require a medium (water) to travel through and involve the actual movement of particles in the medium.

questions.q_en:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?

I. Light waves can be polarized, but sound waves cannot.

II. The Doppler effect occurs due to the relative motion between a wave source and an observer.
questions.solution_en:
Statement I is correct: Light waves are transverse electromagnetic waves, which means their oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of propagation. This allows them to be polarized. Sound waves, however, are longitudinal mechanical waves, where particle vibrations occur along the direction of propagation, so they cannot be polarized.

Statement II is correct: The Doppler effect refers to the change in frequency or wavelength of a wave as perceived by an observer moving relative to the source of the wave. It applies to both sound and electromagnetic waves.

questions.q_en:
Match the following wave properties with their correct descriptions:

PropertyDescription
(A) Frequency(1) Distance between two successive crests/troughs
(B) Amplitude(2) Number of oscillations per second
(C) Wavelength(3) Maximum displacement from mean position
(D) Time period(4) Time taken for one complete cycle
questions.solution_en:
· Frequency is the number of cycles or oscillations a wave completes in one second, measured in Hertz (Hz).

· Amplitude is the maximum displacement of the particles from their mean position in a wave.

· Wavelength is the distance between two consecutive crests or troughs in a transverse wave (or compressions/rarefactions in a longitudinal wave).

· Time period is the time it takes to complete one full cycle of the wave.

questions.q_en: The bending of waves around obstacles is called:
questions.solution_en:
· Diffraction:

o Occurs when waves bend around obstacles or through openings.

o Example: Hearing sound around a corner or light spreading through a slit.

· Why not others?

Reflection: Waves bouncing off a surface (e.g., echo).

Refraction: Change in wave direction due to medium change (e.g., light bending in water).

Polarization: Restriction of wave oscillations to one plane (light waves only).

questions.q_en: A tuning fork produces which type of wave in air?
questions.solution_en:
· Tuning forks create sound waves in air, which are longitudinal waves.

· Longitudinal waves: Air molecules vibrate parallel to the direction of wave propagation, forming compressions and rarefactions.

· When a tuning fork vibrates, it pushes air molecules, creating alternating high-pressure (compression) and low-pressure (rarefaction) regions that travel as sound.

questions.q_en: The equation of a wave is given by y=Asin(ωt−kx). What does k represent?
questions.solution_en:
In the wave equation y=Asin(ωt−kx):

· A is the amplitude of the wave (maximum displacement).

· ω is the angular frequency, related to the frequency f by ω=2πf.

· k is the wave number, which tells us how many radians the wave oscillates per unit distance.

The wave number k is given by:

k=2π/λ​

where λ is the wavelength.

So, k represents the spatial frequency of the wave - how tightly the wave is "packed" in space.

questions.q_en: Which factor does NOT affect the speed of sound in a medium?
questions.solution_en:
The speed of sound in a medium depends on properties like:

· Temperature: Higher temperatures generally increase the speed.

· Density: Denser media can affect how fast sound travels.

· Pressure: In gases, pressure (at constant temperature) doesn't change speed much, but combined with temperature, it has an effect.

However, the color of the medium is not a physical property that affects sound propagation. It's related to how the medium interacts with light, not sound.

questions.q_en: Which phenomenon explains why a person at a distance hears sound even when a barrier is in place?

· Reflection is the bouncing back of waves.

· Refraction is the change in direction due to a change in medium.

· Absorption involves energy loss as sound is absorbed by a material.

questions.q_en: The relation between velocity (v), frequency (f), and wavelength (λ\lambda) of a wave is:
questions.solution_en:
The relation between velocity (v), frequency (f), and wavelength (λ) of a wave is:

v=fλ

Explanation:

· v = wave velocity (how fast the wave travels)

· f = frequency (number of oscillations per second)

· λ = wavelength (distance between two successive crests or troughs)

This formula shows that the speed of a wave is directly proportional to both its frequency and its wavelength.

questions.q_en: When two waves of the same frequency and amplitude interfere constructively, the resultant amplitude is:
questions.solution_en:
· Constructive interference occurs when two waves meet in phase (i.e., their crests and troughs align).

· When the waves have the same frequency and amplitude, their amplitudes add up at every point.

· So, if each wave has amplitude AAA, the resultant wave will have amplitude A+A=2A.
